temple

The Jerusalem temple rebuilt after the exile (completed c. 516 BC) and greatly expanded by Herod, destroyed by Rome in AD 70. 'Second Temple Judaism' also names the Jewish world of c. 516 BC–AD 70 that forms the background of the New Testament.
AD 70
fall of Jerusalem
destruction of Jerusalem
destruction of the temple
Jewish War
70 AD

The year Roman forces under Titus destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, ending the Jewish War (AD 66–70/73). Preterists see it as the fulfilment of many prophecies (the 'coming' in judgment, the great tribulation); all views agree Jesus predicted the temple's fall.
Anno Domini 70.
Papias
Early second-century bishop of Hierapolis whose fragments, preserved by Irenaeus and Eusebius, contain the earliest attested Christian chiliasm (a fruitful earthly kingdom after the resurrection).
Greek personal name.
Montanism
Montanist
New Prophecy

A second-century prophetic movement in Phrygia that claimed new revelations and expected the New Jerusalem to descend nearby. Its intense apocalypticism contributed to suspicion of chiliasm in later centuries.
Named after its founder Montanus.
Joachim of Fiore
Joachimism
Joachimite

Twelfth-century Calabrian abbot (c. 1135–1202) who divided history into ages of the Father, Son and Spirit and expected a coming 'age of the Spirit' within history. His ideas influenced later historicist and optimistic readings of prophecy.
Italian Gioacchino da Fiore.
Darby
Darbyism
Plymouth Brethren leader (1800–1882) regarded as the founder of dispensationalism and of the systematized pretribulational rapture.
Personal name.
Scofield Reference Bible
Scofield Bible
Scofield

A study Bible edited by C. I. Scofield (1909; revised 1917) whose notes popularized dispensationalism, the seven dispensations and the pretribulational rapture throughout English-speaking evangelicalism.
Named after its editor, C. I. Scofield.
Westminster Confession of Faith
Westminster Confession
WCF

The Reformed confession of 1646 whose final chapters (32–33) teach the intermediate state, one general resurrection and one last judgment. It does not define a millennial position; its Larger Catechism (Q. 191) prays for the spread of the gospel and the conversion of the Jews, a text postmillennialists cite.
Composed by the Westminster Assembly, London.
Apostles' Creed
Apostles Creed

An early Western baptismal creed affirming that Christ 'will come to judge the living and the dead' and belief in 'the resurrection of the body'. It is a common measure of eschatological orthodoxy, cited against full preterism.
Developed from the Old Roman Creed (2nd–4th centuries).
Nicene Creed
Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed

The creed of Nicaea (325) as expanded at Constantinople (381), confessing that Christ 'will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead; his kingdom will have no end', and looking for 'the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come'. The phrase about the endless kingdom was added partly against views that limited Christ's reign.
Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
Imminence
imminent
any-moment return

The belief that Christ's return could occur at any moment. Pretribulationists hold that no prophesied events must precede the rapture; other views affirm readiness and nearness while holding that certain events (such as the man of lawlessness or the gospel's spread) come first.
Latin imminere, 'to overhang, be near'.
Day-year principle
year-day principle
day for a year

The historicist rule that a prophetic 'day' symbolizes a year (appealing to Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6), so that the 1,260 days of Revelation 11–12 signify 1,260 years. Most non-historicists reject it outside Daniel 9.
Coming on the clouds
Son of Man coming on the clouds
coming in the clouds

The imagery of Daniel 7:13 used by Jesus (Matthew 24:30; 26:64). Futurists see a visible future return; preterists and N. T. Wright read it, in Daniel's sense, as the Son of Man's vindication and enthronement, manifested in the judgment of AD 70.
Greek erchomenon epi tōn nephelōn.
Future conversion of Israel
all Israel will be saved
conversion of the Jews
national conversion

The expectation, based on Romans 11:25-27, of a future large-scale turning of ethnic Jews to Christ. It is held by dispensationalists, historic premillennialists, many postmillennialists (the Puritan Hope) and some amillennialists; others read 'all Israel' as the full elect remnant through history or the whole church.
Babylon the Great
Babylon
great harlot
the harlot
whore of Babylon

The harlot city of Revelation 17–18. Identified as Rome (the dominant scholarly view), apostate Jerusalem (many preterists), the papacy (historicists), a future world system or rebuilt city (futurists), or the world's seductive system in every age (idealists).
From the ancient city of Babylon, the archetypal oppressor of God's people.
the sealed
twelve tribes sealed

The sealed servants 'from every tribe of the sons of Israel' (Revelation 7:4-8; 14:1-5). Read as Jewish believers in the future tribulation (futurism), first-century Jewish Christians who escaped Jerusalem (preterism), or the whole people of God symbolically numbered (idealism and many amillennialists).
Two witnesses
the two witnesses

The prophetic figures of Revelation 11:3-13 who testify for 1,260 days, are killed and raised. Identified as future individuals (often Moses and Elijah figures), first-century witnesses in Jerusalem, or the witnessing church in every age.
holy city
heavenly Jerusalem

The holy city descending from heaven as the bride of the Lamb (Revelation 21–22; compare Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22). Seen as the final eternal state, the glorified church, or both, already present in principle and fully revealed at the end.
Greek Ierousalēm kainē.
Shekinah
Shekinah glory
shekhinah

A post-biblical rabbinic term for God's dwelling or manifest presence, especially the glory-cloud in the tabernacle and temple. Eschatologically it connects with the promise that God will dwell with his people in the new creation (Revelation 21:3), and with debates over whether a rebuilt temple has a future role.
Hebrew shakan, 'to dwell'; compare Greek skēnoō (John 1:14; Revelation 21:3).
Eschatology: the big picture
The four classic millennial views are distinguished chiefly by how they relate which two things?
The date of Revelation and the identity of the beast
The number of resurrections and the location of heaven
The timing of Christ's return and the nature of the thousand years of Revelation 20
The order of the Gospels and the authorship of Revelation

Premillennialists place the Second Coming before the millennium, postmillennialists after it, and amillennialists read the thousand years of Revelation 20:1-6 as the present age, so 'no future millennium' rather than 'no millennium'.
Why does this study treat preterism, historicism, futurism and idealism separately from the millennial views?
They are approaches to the timing and reference of Revelation's prophecies, and can combine with more than one millennial view
They are four older names for the four millennial views
They are Roman Catholic alternatives to Protestant millennial views
They concern only the book of Daniel, not Revelation

The hermeneutic approaches ask when and to what Revelation's visions refer; for example, partial preterism pairs with postmillennialism (Gentry, Mathison) and with amillennialism, and futurism pairs with both kinds of premillennialism.
What do the ecumenical creeds affirm about the end that all the historic millennial views share?
A literal thousand-year reign on earth after Christ's return
A pretribulational rapture of the church
That the millennium began in AD 70
Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, with the resurrection of the dead
The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds confess Christ's return to judge and the resurrection, but take no position on the millennium; the millennial debate takes place inside that shared creedal core.
Which 1977 multi-view book, edited by Robert G. Clouse, set the modern pattern of comparing millennial views side by side?
Revelation: Four Views
Three Views on the Rapture
When Shall These Things Be?

Clouse's volume had George Eldon Ladd (historic premillennialism), Herman Hoyt (dispensational premillennialism), Loraine Boettner (postmillennialism) and Anthony Hoekema (amillennialism) present and respond to each other.
The phrase 'already and not yet', associated with Geerhardus Vos, Oscar Cullmann and George Ladd, means that
The rapture has already happened for some believers but not for others
The kingdom and the age to come have broken in with Christ's first coming but await consummation at his return
Some prophecies were fulfilled in AD 70 and none remain
The millennium has begun in heaven but will never come on earth

Inaugurated eschatology holds that the 'last days' began with Christ's resurrection and Pentecost (Acts 2:16-17; Hebrews 1:2) while the resurrection of the body and new creation remain future. Nearly every modern view uses some version of it.
Why is Matthew 24:34 ('this generation will not pass away') so central to the debate?
It is the only verse that mentions the millennium
It is missing from the oldest manuscripts
It names the Antichrist
Its time reference shapes whether the Olivet Discourse is read as fulfilled in AD 70, still future, or both

Preterists take 'this generation' as Jesus' contemporaries and see fulfilment in Jerusalem's fall; many futurists read it as 'the generation that sees these signs' or 'this race'; others divide the discourse between AD 70 and the final coming.
Which statement about the date of Revelation is accurate?
It is disputed: most scholars favour c. AD 95 under Domitian, while a significant minority argue for a date before AD 70
All scholars agree it was written in AD 68
It was certainly written after AD 135
The book itself states the year of writing

The late date rests heavily on Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3); early-date advocates such as Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell) and J. A. T. Robinson appeal to internal evidence like the temple in Revelation 11:1-2. The question matters most for preterist readings.
Daniel 9:24-27 (the 'seventy weeks') is a flashpoint mainly because interpreters disagree about
Whether Daniel was written in Greek or Aramaic
Whether the weeks are counted from the Exodus
Whether the seventieth week followed the sixty-ninth directly in Christ's ministry or is separated from it by a gap reaching to the end of the age
Whether the passage mentions the Messiah at all

Dispensationalists see a gap with a future seven-year week (the tribulation); many covenant interpreters see the week fulfilled in Christ's death and the following years, with Jerusalem's destruction as its consequence.
What is 'chiliasm'?
The belief that the world will end in the year 1000
A Latin term for the binding of Satan
The Reformed doctrine of the covenant of works
An older name, from the Greek for 'thousand', for belief in a future earthly millennial reign of Christ
Chiliasm (Greek chilioi, 'thousand'; Latin equivalent millenarianism) describes the premillennial expectation held by early writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.
Where does the word 'rapture' come from?
The Latin rapiemur ('we shall be caught up') in the Vulgate of 1 Thessalonians 4:17
The Hebrew word for 'trumpet' in Joel 2
A nineteenth-century coinage by C. I. Scofield
The Greek title of the book of Revelation

All views believe believers will be 'caught up' to meet the Lord (Greek harpazo). The dispute is over timing: pretribulational, midtribulational, prewrath, posttribulational, or simultaneous with a single final return.
What does postmillennialism hold about the relation of Christ's return to the millennium?
Christ returns before a literal thousand-year reign in Jerusalem
There is no millennium at all, present or future
Christ returns after a long era in which the gospel, through the Spirit, brings the great majority of people and nations to faith
Christ returned spiritually in AD 70 and there is no future coming

Postmillennialists such as Loraine Boettner (The Millennium, 1957) and Kenneth Gentry (He Shall Have Dominion) teach that Christ's kingdom grows through gospel means, issuing in a 'golden age' before a single, visible Second Coming, general resurrection and judgment.
Which parables do postmillennialists commonly cite for the gradual, pervasive growth of the kingdom?
The ten virgins and the talents (Matthew 25)
The mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31-33)
The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31)
The prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32)
The kingdom begins small but grows to fill the field and permeate the whole lump; postmillennialists combine these with Daniel 2:35, where the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth.
How do postmillennialists use Psalm 110:1 together with 1 Corinthians 15:24-26?
They argue Christ will begin to reign only after he returns
They read both texts as fulfilled in Solomon
Christ reigns now from heaven until his enemies are made his footstool, so his return comes at the end of that conquering reign
They hold the enemies are subdued only in heaven, not on earth

Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament text most quoted in the New Testament; postmillennialists stress that Christ sits at the right hand 'until' his enemies are subdued, with death the last enemy destroyed at his coming.
What role did Daniel Whitby (1638-1726) play in the history of postmillennialism?
His 'Treatise of the True Millennium' (1703) popularised a systematic postmillennial scheme, though optimistic views predate him
He founded dispensationalism at Powerscourt
He wrote the Westminster Confession's chapter on the last things
He was the first to teach that the Pope is Antichrist

Critics sometimes call Whitby the 'founder' of postmillennialism; proponents such as Iain Murray (The Puritan Hope) document that Puritans like Thomas Brightman, John Owen and others held hopes of a latter-day spread of the gospel well before him.
Why do postmillennialists often cite the Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 191?
It explicitly defines a thousand-year golden age before Christ's return
It condemns premillennialism by name
It dates Revelation before AD 70
Its exposition of 'Thy kingdom come' asks that the gospel be spread through the world, the Jews called, and the fullness of the Gentiles brought in

The catechism does not adopt a millennial scheme, so the link is an inference; postmillennialists argue that the prayer it teaches expects a worldwide gospel triumph and a future conversion of Israel (Romans 11:25-26).
Which of these figures is a historic representative of postmillennialism?
Anthony Hoekema

Edwards, the Princeton theologians Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, and many nineteenth-century American evangelicals held postmillennial hopes; Darby was a dispensationalist, Hoekema an amillennialist, Ladd a historic premillennialist.
What is commonly given as a reason postmillennialism declined in the early twentieth century?
Its rejection by the Westminster Assembly
The shock of the world wars and its perceived association with the liberal 'social gospel'
The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls
Its condemnation at the Council of Ephesus

Postmillennialists respond that their hope rests on the Spirit's work through the gospel rather than on human progress, and that evangelical postmillennialism differs fundamentally from social-gospel optimism; the view revived from the 1970s through writers such as Rushdoony, Bahnsen, Gentry and Mathison.
Contemporary postmillennialism is often divided into two broad streams. Which pair is correct?
Pretribulational and posttribulational postmillennialism
Historic and progressive postmillennialism
Jewish and Gentile postmillennialism
Revivalist (Puritan/Edwardsean) postmillennialism and theonomic or Reconstructionist postmillennialism

Iain Murray and Keith Mathison represent a revival-centred emphasis, while R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gentry linked postmillennial hope with the application of biblical law to society; many postmillennialists hold neither theonomy nor its rejection as essential.
How did B. B. Warfield interpret Revelation 20:1-10 in 'The Millennium and the Apocalypse' (1904)?
As a vision of the blessed state of saints in heaven during the present age, while he located postmillennial hope in other texts
As a literal thousand years after a future rapture
As fulfilled entirely in the reign of Constantine
As a prediction of the Protestant Reformation

Warfield's reading of Revelation 20 resembles amillennial exegesis; his optimism about the gospel's worldwide victory came from texts such as 1 Corinthians 15 and from Revelation 19's picture of the conquering Word.
How do postmillennialists usually answer the objection that 2 Timothy 3:1-5 and Luke 18:8 predict worsening conditions?
They deny these books are canonical
They agree the world will grow steadily worse until Christ returns
Many read these as describing particular periods (such as the apostolic generation) or as compatible with overall progress that includes setbacks
They apply these verses only to the millennium after Christ returns

Gentry and others argue the 'last days' language often refers to the era beginning with Christ's first coming, and that persecution and apostasy coexist with the long-term advance of the kingdom, as in the parable of the wheat and tares.
What does amillennialism hold about the thousand years of Revelation 20?
They are a literal future era after Christ returns
They never refer to any real period
They ended in AD 70 and nothing has followed
They symbolise the present age between Christ's first and second comings, during which Christ reigns and the saints reign with him
Anthony Hoekema (The Bible and the Future) and Kim Riddlebarger (A Case for Amillennialism) stress that amillennialists affirm a millennium; they deny only a future earthly one.
Which term did Jay E. Adams propose (in a 1959 book later reissued as 'The Time Is at Hand') as a better name than 'amillennialism'?
Inaugurated chiliasm
Covenant eschatology
Adams argued the prefix 'a-' wrongly suggests no millennium; 'realized' signals that the millennium is being realized now. Hoekema likewise noted the term 'amillennialism' is unfortunate.
How do amillennialists interpret the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:2-3?
Satan is entirely inactive during the present age
Satan will be bound only after a future seven-year tribulation
It is a restriction on Satan's ability to deceive the nations and prevent the gospel's spread, accomplished by Christ's first coming
The binding is a metaphor for the end of the Roman Empire
They link it to Matthew 12:29 (binding the strong man), Luke 10:18 and John 12:31-32: the nations, once deceived, can now be reached by the gospel even though Satan still prowls (1 Peter 5:8).
Amillennialists commonly identify the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:5-6 as
The bodily resurrection of believers at a pretribulational rapture
A spiritual reality: either regeneration or, more commonly today, believers' entry into Christ's presence at death
The rebuilding of the temple
The conversion of Israel at the end of the age

Hoekema and Meredith Kline read the scene as the souls of martyrs living and reigning in heaven (Revelation 20:4); premillennialists reply that 'came to life' (ezesan) should mean bodily resurrection in both verses 4 and 5.
Which early theologian's 'City of God' (Book 20) shaped the dominant amillennial reading in the Western church?
Augustine, who had earlier held a form of chiliasm, came to read the thousand years as the church age, building on the Donatist exegete Tyconius; Justin, Irenaeus and Papias were premillennial.
What is 'progressive parallelism' (recapitulation), which many amillennialists apply to Revelation?
The view that Revelation's sections repeatedly cover the whole period between the comings from different angles
The view that Revelation 4-22 is in strict chronological order
The idea that each church in Revelation 2-3 represents a future era
The belief that Revelation repeats Daniel word for word
William Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors identified seven parallel sections; on this reading Revelation 20:1 begins again at the first coming rather than following 19:11-21 chronologically.
Which texts do amillennialists cite for a single general resurrection and judgment at Christ's return?
Revelation 20:4-6 alone
Daniel 9:27 and Ezekiel 40-48
Zechariah 14:4 and Isaiah 65:20
John 5:28-29 and Matthew 25:31-46

Jesus speaks of one 'hour' when all in the tombs come out, some to life and some to judgment, and of a single gathering of the nations; amillennialists see no room for a thousand-year interval between the resurrections.
The 'two-age' structure emphasised by Geerhardus Vos and Kim Riddlebarger holds that
There are two separate peoples of God with two destinies
Scripture contrasts 'this age' and 'the age to come', with the age to come beginning at Christ's return in resurrection and new creation
History is divided into the age of law and the age of grace
The millennium is a third age between this age and the age to come
Texts such as Luke 20:34-36 and Matthew 12:32 put resurrection and the age to come together; amillennialists argue this leaves no slot for a further earthly age after the Second Coming.
How does amillennialism usually regard the course of history before Christ's return?
The world will be almost entirely Christianised
The kingdom grows alongside evil, with suffering and gospel advance both continuing until the end; views range from cautious to optimistic
The church will be removed before a seven-year tribulation
Nothing of significance happens between the comings
The wheat and tares grow together until harvest (Matthew 13:24-30); some amillennialists stress a final apostasy, while others (sometimes called 'optimistic amillennialists') stress gospel growth.
Which Reformation-era confession explicitly rejected the idea of an earthly reign of the saints before the resurrection?
The Westminster Larger Catechism
The Scofield Reference Bible
The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
The Augsburg Confession (Article 17)

Article 17 condemns those spreading 'Jewish opinions' of a worldly kingdom of the godly before the resurrection; the Second Helvetic Confession has a similar rejection. Premillennialists note these were aimed largely at radical Anabaptist movements.
Historic premillennialism
What is the central claim of historic premillennialism?
Christ returns once, after the tribulation, raises believers, and then reigns on earth for a millennium before the final judgment
Christ returns twice: secretly for the church and later with it
The millennium is the present church age
The millennium is a golden age before Christ returns
George Eldon Ladd (The Blessed Hope, 1956) defended a single posttribulational return followed by a millennial reign, without dispensationalism's sharp Israel-church distinction.
Why is the view called 'historic' premillennialism?
It was the official view of the Council of Nicaea
It was invented by historians in the nineteenth century
Proponents argue it resembles the chiliasm of second-century writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus
It interprets Revelation by the day-year principle
Justin's Dialogue with Trypho (80-81) and Irenaeus's Against Heresies Book 5 expected a future reign in a restored Jerusalem; Justin also admitted that some orthodox Christians thought otherwise.
What exegetical argument about Revelation 20:4-5 do historic premillennialists consider decisive?
The word 'thousand' never means a literal number in Greek
The first resurrection refers to Israel's national restoration
The verses are missing from early manuscripts
The same verb, 'came to life' (ezesan), should mean bodily resurrection in both verses, so there are two bodily resurrections separated by the thousand years

Henry Alford famously argued that if the second resurrection is literal the first must be too; Ladd and Craig Blomberg repeat the point. Amillennialists reply that John contrasts a spiritual first resurrection with physical death.
How do historic premillennialists read 1 Corinthians 15:23-24?
As a sequence (Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming, then the end) that leaves room for an interval before the end
As proof that there will be no future resurrection
As fulfilled entirely at Pentecost
As describing a secret rapture before the tribulation

The words 'then' (epeita, eita) can mark intervals, as between Christ's resurrection and his coming; Ladd suggested the millennium falls between 'at his coming' and 'the end'. Critics answer that 'the end' follows the coming directly.
What view of the rapture do most historic premillennialists hold?
Pretribulational: the church is removed seven years before Christ returns
Partial rapture: only watchful believers are taken
Posttribulational: the church goes through the tribulation and is caught up to meet Christ as he comes
No rapture of any kind

Douglas Moo argued the posttribulational view in Three Views on the Rapture (1984), and Robert Gundry's The Church and the Tribulation (1973) is a classic statement; Alan Kurschner's prewrath view is a related variant.
How does George Ladd's understanding of the kingdom of God differ from classic dispensationalism?
He believed the kingdom was offered to Israel and withdrawn until the end
He saw the kingdom as God's reign already inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, not wholly postponed until the millennium
He identified the kingdom with the visible church on earth
He denied that the kingdom has any future aspect
Ladd's The Gospel of the Kingdom and A Theology of the New Testament popularised the 'already and not yet' framework among evangelicals; the millennium is a future stage of a kingdom already present.
How do historic premillennialists typically see the relation of Israel and the church?
Two peoples with permanently separate destinies and programmes
The church has no connection to Old Testament promises
One people of God, while many still expect a future large-scale turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25-26)
Israel will be saved apart from faith in Christ
This continuity is a key difference from dispensationalism; contributors to A Case for Historic Premillennialism (Blomberg and Chung, eds., 2009) argue the case from Scripture and church history.
What purpose do historic premillennialists often give for a millennial reign after Christ's return?
It displays Christ's public victory within history and vindicates God's purposes for the created order before the final state
It allows unbelievers a second chance after the final judgment
It replaces the new heavens and new earth
It exists to rebuild the temple sacrifices for atonement

Proponents such as Ladd and Wayne Grudem argue the reign shows that the curse is partially lifted and Christ's rule is vindicated on earth; critics ask why glorified saints would share the world with mortals.
What is a common amillennial objection to historic premillennialism, and the typical reply?
That it denies the Second Coming; they reply it affirms two comings
That it requires a pre-AD 70 date for Revelation; they reply with Irenaeus
That it rejects Romans 11; they reply by rejecting Romans
That Revelation 20 is the only text teaching an interim kingdom; premillennialists reply that one clear text suffices and that other texts allow for it

Critics stress that no other passage explicitly mentions a thousand-year reign after the parousia; premillennialists answer that Isaiah 65:20, Zechariah 14 and 1 Corinthians 15 fit such an interval and that Scripture need only say something once.
Dispensational premillennialism
Which sequence best summarises dispensational premillennialism?
Gospel growth, golden age, Christ's return, final judgment
Pretribulational rapture, seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week), Christ's return, a literal thousand-year reign centred on Israel
Church age, single return, general resurrection, new creation
AD 70 parousia, eternal kingdom, no further return
Classic statements include J. Dwight Pentecost's Things to Come (1958) and John Walvoord's The Rapture Question (1957) and The Millennial Kingdom.
Which figure, associated with the Plymouth Brethren and the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-1833), systematised dispensational teaching?
Daniel Whitby
Lady Theodosia Powerscourt hosted prophecy conferences at her Wicklow estate, where Darby developed his distinction between Israel and the church and a pretribulational 'catching up' of the church.
What made the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) so influential?
It was the first English translation of the Bible
It was the official Bible of the Church of England
It introduced the day-year principle
Its notes carried dispensational premillennialism into a widely used study Bible across English-speaking evangelicalism

C. I. Scofield's notes (Oxford University Press; revised 1917 and 1967) divided history into seven dispensations and taught a pretribulational rapture; Dallas Theological Seminary (founded 1924 by Lewis Sperry Chafer) carried the tradition forward.
How do dispensationalists read Daniel 9:26-27?
The seventieth week is separated from the sixty-ninth by the church age and will be fulfilled in a future seven-year tribulation
The seventieth week ended at the crucifixion with no gap
The seventy weeks are symbolic of the whole of world history
The passage refers only to Antiochus Epiphanes

The 'he' who confirms a covenant (Daniel 9:27) is read as the coming Antichrist; critics argue the text gives no gap and that 'he' is Messiah, while dispensationalists point to prophetic gaps elsewhere (e.g. Isaiah 61:1-2 in Luke 4:18-19).
Which text is the primary description of the rapture for dispensationalists?

All views accept the 'catching up' of 1 Thessalonians 4:17; pretribulationists add arguments from promises of deliverance from wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9; Revelation 3:10) and from the church's absence from Revelation 4-19.
Why is 'imminence' important to the pretribulational argument?
It shows the rapture happened in AD 70
It proves the millennium is the present age
